ideas.solution: A neutral party, under family consent, holds the award ledger and eligibility credential; platforms and SGOs call an API before awarding; one verification is reusable (categorical eligibility, direct income documents, safe-harbor flags); states get dashboards.
ideas.why_now: The proposed regulation appeared 1 Oct 2026; SGOs must stand up procedures for 2027; 600-700 SGOs by 2030 (S).
ideas.wedge: The ten largest new SGOs in Texas, Florida and Georgia plus one platform partner for duplicate checks; the Texas waitlist (~153,000, S) as the first eligibility pool.
ideas.path_to_100m: Central case: 0.63M ECCA recipients ($5B / $8,000 blended) + ~2.5M state-program recipients (A) = 3.1M x $12 = $37M; 2.5M credentials x $10 = $25M; 30 states x $1M analytics = $30M. Total ~$92M, which needs nearly every recipient on the rail (a winner-take-most standard). Treasury case: ~6M recipients x $12 + 5M credentials x $10 + $30M = ~$152M, ~66% of recipients. Analog: the National Student Clearinghouse reaches $102.5M revenue (S).
ideas.who_does_it_today: No cross-platform registry found. In-house checks at each SGO and platform; Equifax Work Number at $46.95 per employer record (S); IRS IVES and payroll-data aggregators (U); the National Student Clearinghouse covers postsecondary only. Odyssey's SGO page and FACTS Compass's announcement do not mention anti-duplication (S).
ideas.why_they_lose: The platforms are direct rivals and will not pool award data; states are bound by their own statutes; a nonprofit SGO has no budget for a data product inside its overhead cap.
ideas.moat: Network economies and a standard; switching costs; a data asset no single platform can build.
ideas.earned_secret: The only cross-program control today is a call between program staff (insider hypothesis, U). The sourced fact is structural: the rule mandates cross-award duplicate detection yet creates no shared registry, and the competing platforms have a conflict that blocks them from building one.
ideas.first_90_days: Comment on the proposed regulation asking Treasury to treat a shared registry as a 'reasonable procedure'; build the ledger API with two SGOs; sign one platform partner; design the consent flow.

ideas.title: Family-facing funding stack and net-price front door (Common App for choice dollars)
ideas.one_liner: One free application and net-price screen that shows a family every ESA, voucher, SGO scholarship and school aid it qualifies for, school by school, and submits once; paid per funded student by SGOs and per enrolled student by schools.
ideas.customer: Families (free); SGOs and schools pay.
ideas.payer_and_signer: SGO pays ~$100 per awarded student (cheaper than Treasury's ~$100 income verification, S); schools pay ~$300 per new enrolled student (A). Signer: SGO development director; school head or admissions director.
ideas.problem: Texas had ~274,000 applications for ~85,000-107,000 funded seats and ~153,000 waitlisted (S); awards of $10,474 (S) meet tuition that may be higher (A), and families cannot see net price after stacking. SGOs, once they have raised money, must spend 90% of income by the end of the next year (S) and need verified applicants, while donors may give to any participating state (S).
ideas.solution: An eligibility engine and net-price calculator across programs; a single intake routed to each payer reusing the credential from idea 5; a waitlist exchange (Texas participates in the federal credit, S, so 2027 SGO dollars can fund waitlisted children).
ideas.why_now: Texas's waitlist meets the first federal-credit scholarship season (2027-28).
ideas.wedge: Texas waitlisted families, three Texas SGOs and ten private schools with open seats.
ideas.path_to_100m: 0.6M funded students/yr through the platform x $100 = $60M, plus 0.15M new-to-school students x $300 = $45M = ~$105M. That is ~55% of roughly 1.1M newly funded students per year (A): heroic. Better treated as a funnel that feeds ideas 3 and 5.
ideas.who_does_it_today: State school-finder portals, Odyssey and ClassWallet application flows, Step Up's own application, FACTS Grant & Aid (S); Niche, GreatSchools and SchoolMint-type enrollment tools (U).
ideas.why_they_lose: Each payer can only promote its own pot: state agencies cannot advertise SGO scholarships or other states' programs, SGOs market only themselves, schools market sticker price, platforms are paid by states, and FACTS Grant & Aid is paid by schools and sees only aid. Only a neutral party can show the stack.
ideas.moat: Two-sided network economies; data on net price. Thin.
ideas.earned_secret: The family does not need more school reviews, it needs the stack; and SGOs will find that applicant supply, not donor dollars, binds once the 90% test is running. Both are hypotheses (U). A smart generalist would think of this in five minutes, which is why it scores low.
ideas.first_90_days: Texas waitlist pilot with one SGO and ten schools; measure cost per funded student versus the $100 verification baseline.

ideas.title: Permitted-seat platform (E-occupancy landlord and turnkey seats)
ideas.one_liner: Convert closing school buildings and church education wings into permitted 100-seat schools once, then sell turnkey seats to microschool operators on long leases backed by the ESA and SGO payment stream.
ideas.customer: Microschool and small-school operators (about 75,000 microschools, median 20 students, S); on the supply side, church trustees and diocesan CFOs.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Operator pays ~$2,900 per seat per year (about 28% of a $10.5k award, A) for facility, furniture, insurance, safety systems and payment rail. Signer: operator founder; landlord side, pastor or diocesan CFO.
ideas.problem: Texas launched TEFA on 1 Jul 2026 with ~274,000 applications against ~85,000-107,000 funded seats, ~153,000 waitlisted, and the Comptroller wants $2B (S). Microschools are limited by occupancy and zoning: Utah's 2026 law caps a facility at 100 students tied to occupancy codes (S), a Utah city requires Group E occupancy (S), and funders such as the Stand Together/Building Hope microschool fund require a signed commercial lease first (S).
ideas.solution: Master-lease or acquire; do the occupancy, fire and zoning conversion once; deliver standardized 100-seat sites to operators; collect rent through the wallet sweep (idea 3).
ideas.why_now: Money is abundant and seats are not: 63 Catholic schools closed in 2024-25 (S) while Texas has a six-figure waitlist; federal-credit scholarships arrive in 2027.
ideas.wedge: Three Texas sites with two operators, then Arizona, Florida and Tennessee; one lender for conversion capex.
ideas.path_to_100m: 34,000 seats x $2,900 = ~$99M, i.e. 340 sites x 100 seats and ~22% of Texas's waitlist alone (A). Capital need $15-30M working capital and conversion capex in a master-lease model (A), far more if buying.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Operators lease churches one at a time; Prenda is home-based and asset-light; KaiPod takes a 10% two-year revenue share (S); CDFIs and Building Hope finance after a lease exists (S); churches lease directly. I found no scaled school-use landlord.
ideas.why_they_lose: Asset-light operators cannot hold leases or conversion risk because their investors fund software; dioceses cannot operate; CDFIs lend only after a lease; commercial landlords will not convert space for a 20-student tenant.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (permitted buildings in the right metros) and process power in permitting.
ideas.earned_secret: The scarce asset is a permitted building, not a teacher or curriculum. That facility scarcity at the margin is an inference (U): nearly 40% of Catholic schools have waiting lists (S) but others have room.
ideas.first_90_days: Map 150 closing or under-used school buildings in Texas; sign three sites and two operators; price conversion capex with an architect and fire marshal.

ideas.title: Credit concierge (free planning tool for tax professionals and payroll, paid by SGOs)
ideas.one_liner: Make a $1,700 gift to a scholarship organization cost the donor nothing by planning it with their CPA or payroll team: capacity, state-credit stacking, W-4 offset and payroll deduction.
ideas.customer: Tax preparers, CPAs and enrolled agents; payroll and HR administrators at employers in the 30 participating states; donors reached through both.
ideas.payer_and_signer: SGOs pay the platform ~6% of each completed gift (A); the tool is free to CPAs and employers. Signer: SGO development director or executive director.
ideas.problem: The credit is nonrefundable, so donors need $1,700 of liability; the donor pays cash before the credit; stacking with state credits changes the net outcome; Treasury estimates 46.5M taxpayers could use both state and federal credits and at 10% take-up about 3.1M (plus 1.55M more married filers) would net up to $1,700 or $3,400 (S). Arizona individual giving fell ~23% in a year (S), so habit must be built.
ideas.solution: A free calculator for CPAs (client-by-client credit capacity, state stacking, carryforward, W-4 or estimated-tax adjustment, SGO shortlist by state), an employer payroll-giving connector, and a donor flow that handles Form 8525 donor numbers and 31 Jan acknowledgments for the SGO. No commissions to CPAs (AICPA commission rules, U); flat SGO-paid fee on completed gifts. Donors may rely on the IRS SGO list at the time of the gift (S), so no donor-side diligence is needed.
ideas.why_now: The credit starts 1 Jan 2027; Treasury expects 11M donors and $26B/yr by 2030 (S); payroll deduction is an explicitly allowed contribution method (S).
ideas.wedge: 200 CPA firms in Texas, Florida and Georgia; three payroll or PEO partners; five SGOs as payers.
ideas.path_to_100m: Central case: $5B x 30% intermediated = $1.5B x 6% = ~$90M; $100M needs about a third of all central-case giving through the tool (heroic). Treasury case: $26B x 30% x 4% = ~$312M. Grounding for $5B: Arizona individual STO giving of $86-112M over ~3.3M returns is $26-34 per return, times ~160M US returns = $4.2-5.4B (A, mature-market ceiling; realistic 2027-28 is $1-2B).
ideas.who_does_it_today: SGOs' own donor teams; workplace-giving platforms such as Benevity and Givebutter with no SGO support found (S); payroll providers (none found); Intuit (U). No planning tool exists.
ideas.why_they_lose: SGOs cannot afford tax-advisor outreach inside 10-15% overhead (fundraising counts against the 85% activity test, S); giving platforms do not give tax advice; payroll companies avoid charity; tax software acts after the year-end deadline (U).
ideas.moat: Distribution into preparer and payroll workflows (switching costs) and data on donor capacity.
ideas.earned_secret: The giving decision is made by the advisor in Q3-Q4, not by the donor in Feb-April. W-4 Step 3 lets an employee add 'the value of any other credits', which reduces withholding (S), so a payroll gift can be cash-neutral; Treasury has not endorsed that pattern (U; only a 74 Million commentary proposes it). That advisors decide is an insider hypothesis (U).
ideas.first_90_days: Sign three SGOs as payers; build the calculator; recruit 50 CPA firms by 15 Dec; file a comment asking Treasury to confirm that payroll-deduction gifts plus W-4 Step 3 is an acceptable cash-neutral pattern.

ideas.title: Parity
ideas.one_liner: A fixed-price, date-certain conversion assurance and migration engine that rebuilds how an institution actually runs (from configs, exam findings, tickets, call recordings, staff walk-throughs), proves account-by-account parity before cutover, and keeps every source-to-target mapping as a reusable library.
ideas.customer: The acquirer's COO or Chief Integration Officer when the target's core differs from its own; a $0.5-10B bank or credit union switching cores; and challenger cores (Maximum, 10x, Nymbus, Corelation, Mambu) that need to onboard banks faster.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The 'conversion and integration costs' line of a deal budget, or the technology budget, signed by the COO or CIO with CEO/board sign-off. On the challenger side, the VP of Implementation pays per live bank out of cost of sales.
ideas.problem: A conversion takes 12-22 months (Cornerstone cites a 22-month project). Parity testing runs in Excel by two or three staff who also run the bank. The old vendor hands over flat files with an incomplete data dictionary, on its own schedule and price list (one consultant saw $200k quoted to deconvert 10,000 accounts). The defects that hurt customers come from rules nobody wrote down.
ideas.solution: Ingest the old core's parameter files, extracts, policies, exam reports, tickets and recorded staff walk-throughs; agents write a behaviour spec (product rules, fee/interest logic, GL mapping, custom reports, exceptions); generate target-core setup and data mapping; run repeated mock conversions through an automated parity harness (balances, accrued interest, holds, fees, statements, tax forms) and issue a signed parity report boards and examiners can read; price per account with a go-live date, backed by an insurer-funded warranty (design, not yet agreed). Not the 'COBOL to Java' cliche: the product is behaviour parity between two cores.
ideas.why_now: Bank deals are still 83 (H1 2026) to 117 (H2 2025) a half-year; the FDIC voted 17 Sep 2026 to propose faster merger review; Fiserv is losing share and reviewing its portfolio; AI-native cores (Maximum at Emprise Bank, 10x with AI Migrate) show challengers can run phased migrations, which makes conversion capacity the bottleneck; models can now read legacy configs and transcripts.
ideas.wedge: Independent parity assurance for acquirers in announced deals where the two cores differ. The vendor still does the load, so Parity displaces no one. First 10 customers: ten acquirers of $0.5-3B targets found from deal filings that name cores and conversion dates, at about $250k each, plus 3-4 CU mergers.
ideas.path_to_100m: Core conversions run 500-1,000 a year (ICBA: 36% of community banks changed core within 5 years, about 7%/yr; FIntegrate: average FI converts every 8.5 years, about 1,020/yr across about 8,660 FIs). Revenue about $350k per core conversion (assurance $150k + engine $200k, roughly 20-25% of an assumed $1.5-2M all-in cost) and about $100k per digital/card/lending conversion (assumed 0.8 per core conversion). At 25% of all conversions: 125-250 x $350k = $44-88M plus $8-16M ancillary = $52-104M. HEROIC: it needs about 25% of all conversions; standalone bank-side market is $200-400M. Share needed falls if cheaper conversions raise the switch rate (ABA: 19% of banks likely to convert at renewal), and the idea only clears the bar combined with Sunset (vendor-paid volume) and per-live-bank challenger licences.
ideas.who_does_it_today: FIntegrate (Birmingham; FusionLRS launched Jul 2024, legacy images/data research, claims 70% cheaper data conversion, DCI partner Aug 2025, says 4,800 FIs served) covers archives, not rules or parity. Cornerstone Advisors (32 conversions in 2023, 31 engagements in 2024) is project management. Plante Moran, Crowe, Wipfli sell PMO hours (memory). Fiserv, FIS, Jack Henry run their own conversion teams. 10x AI Migrate maps onto 10x only. Mechanical Orchard does mainframe code. No independent AI parity product found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Vendors earn from lock-in and deconversion fees and cannot certify their own conversion; consultants bill by the hour; FIntegrate moves data but does not recover rules; a challenger's tool is a sales aid for its own core.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (the source-by-target mapping library grows with every conversion and nobody else sees as many pairs) plus process power (verified parity pipeline); counter-positioning against vendors who cannot cheapen conversion without weakening lock-in.
ideas.earned_secret: Conversions do not fail on data extraction. They fail on rules nobody wrote down (how a 1998 savings product accrues interest, which custom report the CFO uses) and on the two staff who know them. The schedule is set by those people's hours.
ideas.first_90_days: Build the list of 2025-26 deals naming both cores and a conversion date (S-4/8-K text). Get two institutions that finished a conversion in the last year to let you replay pre/post extracts through the harness and publish the defect classes found. Hire two ex-vendor conversion analysts (Fiserv's restructuring is a talent supply). Quote the first three live deals at a fixed price per account band. Legal check: vendor licences may restrict sharing proprietary data dictionaries; bank owns its data and configs, interagency third-party guidance expects an exit plan (memory); needs counsel.

ideas.title: Tenancy
ideas.one_liner: Run the whole back office of several hundred small credit unions on one multi-tenant stack with shared specialists, so each keeps its own board, brand and charter and pays per member per month instead of per institution plus six salaries.
ideas.customer: CEO and board of a $50-500M credit union (about 3,466 of the 4,214 federally insured CUs are under $500M, derived from NCUA: 748 are over $500M).
ideas.payer_and_signer: The CU's operating budget (staff plus vendor lines; total operating cost about 3% of assets, assumed and not sourced this run). The CEO signs, the board approves.
ideas.problem: CU count fell from 4,411 (Q1 2025) to 4,250 (Q1 2026), about 3.7% a year, because a sub-scale CU must carry a BSA officer, compliance, accounting, IT, lending operations, a core, a digital vendor and a card processor. Merger is the standard answer and it ends independence. The big three price per institution and run single-tenant instances, so three CUs cannot share one.
ideas.solution: A for-profit operator, structured as a CUSO owned by anchor CUs, running a modern multi-tenant core and digital stack, card and lending operations, BSA monitoring, accounting and compliance with AI-run workflows and a pooled team of human specialists. Priced per member per month ($3-4 all-in, assumed) with outcome terms on cost-to-income and exam findings.
ideas.why_now: Fiserv's CEO admitted lost share 'especially on the smaller credit union side' and 'pricing competition' (Fiserv has 1,155 CUs, down from 27.1% to 25.9% share); CU count is dropping fast; rate stress squeezes CU margins; the FDIC proposal puts CUs inside merger competition analysis; agents make shared-service workflows cheap enough that specialists, not tools, are the constraint.
ideas.wedge: Start with the roles small CUs cannot staff well: BSA/AML monitoring, accounting close and exam preparation, for 25 CUs under $150M, ideally ones with a vacancy in the BSA or compliance seat. Add core and digital at the next contract end, using Parity to convert.
ideas.path_to_100m: 200 CUs x about $500k a year ($3.5 x 12,000 members x 12) = $100M, which is 5.8% of the 3,466 CUs under $500M. The unit economics are credible; pace is the risk, since CU boards decide slowly and each core exit needs a conversion. Expect 5-6 years.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Hidden incumbents that prove demand: CU*SOUTH (runs core platforms for member CUs), Xtend (69-75 CU owners), Aux (55 CU owners; accounting, compliance, analytics), CU*Answers (long-running CU-owned shared core, from memory). CU-specific cores (Corelation, FLEX, Sharetec, FedComp, CompuSource) sell software, not a shared back office. I found no CUSO past a few dozen owners.
ideas.why_they_lose: Owner-governed CUSOs move at the speed of their slowest owner and lack capital for a large build. Fiserv and Jack Henry would be selling a CU a cheaper operation that cancels their own per-institution licences, and an outsourced seat competes with their own BPO.
ideas.moat: Scale economies (one stack, one specialist pool), switching costs (the staff are gone, so leaving means rehiring), network economies (pooled fraud and credit signals across hundreds of CUs).
ideas.earned_secret: CU CEOs do not resist mergers over technology. They resist losing the board, the brand and the name on the building. Nobody sells the third option: keep the charter and share everything else.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign 10 design partners at cost for BSA monitoring and accounting; recruit three anchor CUs as CUSO owners; write the services agreement and exam-readiness pack with a CU-experienced law firm; price on per-member bands. Legal check (memory, needs counsel): NCUA CUSO rules (12 CFR 712) allow service CUSOs and NCUA's vendor-oversight authority is limited; the BSA officer is named by the board and stays accountable even when work is shared.

ideas.title: Quorum
ideas.one_liner: A free price-and-peer engine for bank and CU executives (what did a $2B bank on DNA actually pay and get?) built from banks' own invoices and contract abstracts, paid for by vendors who buy disclosed, qualified shortlist slots, with committed-volume group buying as phase two.
ideas.customer: CFO, COO and CEO at the roughly 8,660 FIs, free of charge. The paying buyer is the vendor's CRO or VP of Marketing.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The vendor's customer-acquisition budget (assumed 6% of first-year contract value for a qualified shortlist slot); banks pay nothing. Signer: vendor CRO or VP Marketing.
ideas.problem: Prices are opaque, contracts carry confidentiality clauses, one bank cannot generate a credible competing bid, and notice windows get missed. A 2013-14 BPI Network study (using Paladin data, so biased) put the premium paid at about 24% above fair market. Fiserv is now in retention mode, so a concession window is open.
ideas.solution: Banks upload invoices and contracts; AI abstracts and normalises them per account and per transaction and returns a benchmark, a notice-window calendar and an RFP draft. The answer engine names three vendors with a visible 'sponsored' label. Phase two pools FIs into blocks (100+ institutions committing to a challenger's price card) with a disclosed admin fee paid by the vendor, the healthcare group-purchasing pattern.
ideas.why_now: Invoice abstraction became cheap; Fiserv needs retention (banking services -4%, guide cut to -1% to flat); AI-native challengers (Maximum, 10x) need cheap access to buyers.
ideas.wedge: 30 FIs inside their notice window get a free renewal-leverage report; the first three paying vendors are challengers buying qualified shortlist slots.
ideas.path_to_100m: Competitive core, digital and card decisions run 500-1,000 a year at an assumed $1.2M annual value, so $0.6-1.2B of value; 6% is $36-72M even at 100% capture. Group-purchase admin fees at 3% on 15% of an assumed $9B community big-three spend add about $40M. This is the weakest idea on size: it needs most competitive decisions plus an ancillary pool I could not size from sources. Likely dead as a standalone company; better as the distribution layer for Parity, Sunset and Day One.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Golden Contract Coalition (Paladin fs, Austin, with Pillsbury; launched June 2016; member-paid standard master agreement; close to 50 members and over $1B of contract revenue at launch; 'does not negotiate price'; no 2024-25 data found, so a decade-old boutique). Cornerstone and other core-selection consultants (about $75-250k an RFP, assumed). ICBA/ABA endorsed-vendor programmes, Bank Director FinXTech, G2/Gartner (all from memory). No vendor-paid, invoice-based price engine found.
ideas.why_they_lose: Consultants and the Coalition are paid by banks per project and cannot become free. Vendors cannot publish their own prices. Trade media sell attention, not price data.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (a contract and price database nobody else can assemble) and network economies (more banks, better benchmarks, more vendors), weakened by easy copying once the data exists.
ideas.earned_secret: The leverage is not the price list. It is a credible alternative bid and the notice date. A single bank can produce neither; pooled, anonymised data can.
ideas.first_90_days: Build the invoice-abstraction pipeline on 20 real bank invoices; publish a free Fiserv-renewal leverage guide; sell three shortlist slots to challengers. Legal check (needs counsel): contract confidentiality clauses may bar sharing pricing, so use only the bank's own data and show aggregates; vendor-pays touches the Bank Bribery Act (18 USC 215, from memory) if any value reaches a bank employee or agent, so fees go only to the platform and are disclosed.

ideas.title: Sunset
ideas.one_liner: Outcome-priced migration as a service for the incumbents themselves: a fixed price per account moved from a platform the vendor wants to retire onto its strategic platform, with a no-churn guarantee, so Fiserv, FIS or Jack Henry can finally prune the second and third cores they carry.
ideas.customer: The president of a vendor's financial-institutions business, or its head of client delivery.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The vendor's cost of sales for implementation and conversions (plus a restructuring reserve), signed by the divisional COO. Price per account moved, assumed $15-40.
ideas.problem: Vendors carry overlapping cores for decades because a forced migration is a free RFP for the customer. Fiserv now says 'we need to simplify', is 'reviewing the mix of businesses', has spun off ATMs and sold student-loan servicing, and is weighing a debit-network sale.
ideas.solution: The Parity engine sold on the vendor's side: behaviour recovery, mapping, parity proofs, plus Day One so customers do not re-enrol. Contracts are per account moved, with a guarantee that parity differences are fixed at our cost and a shared retention clause.
ideas.why_now: A new CEO (since mid-June 2026) and a -1% to flat guide make platform rationalisation more likely than in years. This is an inference: I found NO announced core sunset; the American Banker headline says only that product changes may follow.
ideas.wedge: Start with whichever vendor announces a retirement; failing that, the small-CU platforms where Fiserv admits losses. One vendor is the first customer, so concentration is built in; the first ten are ten platform cohorts at that vendor.
ideas.path_to_100m: If Fiserv retires platforms covering 30% of its roughly 3,000 bank and CU clients (assumed from 42% of 4,450 banks plus 1,155 CUs), that is about 900 FIs x $350k of vendor-borne conversion cost = $315M over four years, about $80M a year. FIS and Jack Henry rationalisations and challenger onboarding add the rest. It rests on vendor decisions I could not confirm and on one buyer; I put the core scenario at roughly one in three.
ideas.who_does_it_today: The vendors' own conversion teams plus systems integrators (Cognizant, Tata, Infosys and similar, from memory); FIntegrate on archives; Cornerstone as PMO. Nobody sells outcome-priced, parity-proven migration to vendors.
ideas.why_they_lose: In-house teams are paid per project and their incentive is lock-in; integrators bill time. An outside party with a churn guarantee carries a risk the vendor cannot price internally.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (the mapping library) and switching costs (once a vendor routes retirements through the pipeline it is hard to unwind).
ideas.earned_secret: Vendors do not avoid sunsets because they love old code. They avoid them because customers leave when forced to move. Remove the pain and a sunset becomes affordable.
ideas.first_90_days: Build an end-of-life watchlist from Fiserv, FIS and Jack Henry release notes and customer forums; pitch each vendor's head of delivery with a proof run on a retired-platform client; offer the first migration at cost. Legal risk is low (licence and consent terms sit in the vendor's own contracts); the real checks are customer concentration and revenue recognition.

ideas.title: Books of Record
ideas.one_liner: A vendor-neutral, always-on copy of the bank's ledger and customer records, built from the core's own journals and owned by the bank. It gives 24/7 balance truth and stand-in processing for instant payments, then feeds data and AI, then becomes the control that lets any new core take accounts in cohorts.
ideas.customer: COO or CIO of a $1-10B bank or $1B+ CU (748 CUs are over $500M per NCUA; banks at $1-10B estimated at 700-800, unsourced).
ideas.payer_and_signer: The payments-modernisation, resilience and data-platform budget, $80-250k a year (assumed), signed by the COO or CIO; the board reads it as the exit plan.
ideas.problem: The bank does not hold its own books. The core is nightly batch; every examiner request and analytics project starts with a vendor extract; 24/7 payments need a real-time balance, hold and sanctions check inside seconds (a Federal Reserve comment letter flags real-time OFAC/AML screening inside FedNow's five-second window as a major challenge for smaller institutions); a vendor outage leaves the bank blind; leaving means an 18-month data project. Data-processing cost doubled at Webster Five in five years ($1.23M to $2.49M) and 47% of banks say they are dissatisfied with their core (ABA, via vendor release).
ideas.solution: Event/journal adapters per core (Fiserv Premier, DNA, Portico; FIS Horizon, IBS; Jack Henry SilverLake, Symitar; CSI NuPoint, platform names from memory) feed a canonical immutable double-entry ledger. On top: real-time balance and hold API; stand-in authorisation for FedNow, RTP and cards while the core is in batch or down; continuous reconciliation; examiner-ready reports; a warehouse for AI; one-click exit-plan export. Later, dual-run routing so Maximum, 10x, Thought Machine or Nymbus can take cohorts of accounts with the mirror as control.
ideas.why_now: FedNow/RTP make 24/7 mandatory for anyone who joins; Fiserv's distress makes boards ask about vendor-failure plans; AI-native cores (Maximum at Emprise: phased, existing systems in parallel) need a safe bridge; interagency third-party guidance (June 2023, from memory) expects exit planning.
ideas.wedge: Real-time balance and stand-in for FedNow/RTP at ten banks whose cores post in batch, about $100k each. Second door: challengers (Maximum, 10x, Nymbus) each need a parallel-run bridge to close their next ten banks and can pay per live bank.
ideas.path_to_100m: Land 400 FIs at $150k = $60M, then move 40 of them to ledger-of-record at about $1M = $40M, over 6-7 years. That is about 27% of roughly 1,500 target FIs, which is heroic. The real route is the expansion: once the mirror is the book of record the price moves toward core level ($1-3M for a $2B bank, assumed), so about 70 banks gets to $100M.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Fiserv's Finxact (adjacent next-gen core, tied to Fiserv); Thought Machine, 10x, Mambu (cores with coexistence modes); Volante (raised $66M; payments hub for mid-tier banks; date unconfirmed); Finzly and ACI (payments hubs), Jack Henry's FedNow service, Sheltered Harbor-style data vaults (from memory). Two searches found no neutral mirror for community banks.
ideas.why_they_lose: A batch core cannot be sold as optional and vendors charge for extracts; a neutral mirror weakens lock-in, so no incumbent will build it; Finxact serves Fiserv's strategy; challenger cores want to replace, not mirror; payments hubs do not own the ledger.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (becomes the second, then first, book of record), counter-positioning against vendors, process power (adapters accumulate per core version).
ideas.earned_secret: The board and the examiner believe the bank has its books. In fact every number comes from a vendor extract, and the real reconciliation runs in Excel.
ideas.first_90_days: Map journal/event access on Premier, DNA, SilverLake, Symitar and one more; get two banks to sign data-access letters; build the canonical ledger with 12 months of history for one bank; run a Friday-5pm demo of balance truth against the core. Open legal question: the bank needs a contractual right to near-real-time journals or events, and I do not know which cores expose event streams at all; test first.

ideas.title: Day One
ideas.one_liner: Move each customer's financial graph (bill-pay payees and schedules, direct deposits, card-on-file tokens, external-account links, alerts, Zelle/P2P enrolment) before conversion day, so there is no re-enrolment cliff and first-month attrition collapses.
ideas.customer: The acquirer's head of retail banking or customer experience (M&A) and the switching bank's COO; second market: fintechs and neobanks that want primary accounts.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The merger-integration budget or a deposit-retention reserve. At an assumed 4% marginal funding cost, keeping 6 points of deposits on a $1.5B target ($90M) is worth about $3.6M a year. Price $250-400k a deal, signed by the head of retail with the COO.
ideas.problem: Average deposit attrition after conversion is 11.1% (Curinos), the worst quartile about 17%, the best under 5%; about two-thirds of leavers go in month one (Deloitte). Typical pain: every customer must re-enrol for online banking, Bill Pay and Zelle are down for the weekend, 18,750 calls in two weeks at one bank. The old vendor has no reason to help customers leave, the new vendor cannot see old credentials until cutover, and the bank sits in between.
ideas.solution: With customer consent, capture the graph before cutover (permissioned aggregator access, payroll connections, card networks' account-updater programmes, from memory); pre-provision the new app so day-one login works; carry payees and schedules across; flag at-risk customers (low balance, high fee, inactive) for week-one outreach.
ideas.why_now: Deposits are expensive (a reported 5.35% ten-year yield, single secondary source, unverified), approvals are getting faster (FDIC proposal 17 Sep 2026), and AI-native cores want a clean cutover.
ideas.wedge: Sold with Parity into deals where the target's digital vendor changes. Ten acquirers from filings, one pilot cohort each.
ideas.path_to_100m: Events needing graph migration: about 190 bank deals plus about 150 CU mergers (CU count fell by 161 in the year to Q1 2026, including liquidations) = 340, plus 400-800 voluntary core switches and about 300 digital-only conversions (assumed) = roughly 1,000-1,400 a year. At $250k a deal, 25% share = 250-350 events = $62-88M. A second leg, the same rail used for ordinary primary-account switching at $12 a switch for 3M switches, adds $36M. So $100M needs about 25% of conversion events plus the second leg. HEROIC; the M&A-only version is $20-40M.
ideas.who_does_it_today: The FI's own communications team plus the new vendor's conversion staff (Fiserv, Jack Henry, Alkami, Q2, from memory); Visa/Mastercard account-updater programmes for card-on-file (partial); payroll-connectivity firms (Pinwheel, Atomic, Argyle, from memory) for direct-deposit switching, sold mainly to neobanks; Curinos for benchmarks and advisory. Nobody packages the whole graph for conversions.
ideas.why_they_lose: The old vendor is leaving, the new vendor starts at cutover, consultants sell advice, and payroll-switch firms do one leg.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (a payee, biller and token map that grows with every conversion) plus process power, with network effects as payroll and biller connections accumulate.
ideas.earned_secret: Attrition is not a communications problem. It is the dozen invisible connections (payees, direct deposit, tokens) that silently break. The causal story is my inference; the size comes from Curinos and Deloitte.
ideas.first_90_days: Take two recent conversions and decompose attrition (accounts that lost payees or deposits versus the rest) from the banks' own data; build payee and token capture on one cooperating bank's customers; pilot at 60 days before cutover on an announced deal. Legal check: credential handling and consent under GLBA; with 1033 not in force there is no right to pull data from the old bank, so it runs on the bank's authority plus customer permission; direct-deposit changes need the employee's authorisation.

ideas.title: Switchboard
ideas.one_liner: Open-book, cost-plus debit and card processing for banks and CUs under $10B, with pre-certified multi-network routing so no community institution depends on one network owner, plus an optional cooperative-equity layer for FIs that want to own the plumbing.
ideas.customer: Head of cards or payments and the COO or CFO at a bank or CU under $10B; CU CEOs for smaller shops.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The card-processing line, paid out of interchange (exempt non-prepaid interchange was $14.87B in 2023). COO or CFO signs.
ideas.problem: In July 2026 the WSJ and Reuters reported preliminary talks between several large banks (JPMorgan, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, PNC named) and Fiserv about buying one of its PIN-debit networks (STAR or Accel); the CEO says a sale is under consideration, Cantor expects Accel to be shed, Raymond James expects regulatory scrutiny; no signed deal (secondary summaries). Community FIs enable these networks on their cards; a megabank owner would be a competitor of its users. Processing is bundled into core contracts, pass-throughs and incentives are opaque, and the Fed shows network fees rising to $12.95B ($0.129 a transaction) while exempt average interchange is flat at $0.52, so the squeeze falls on issuer and processor.
ideas.solution: (1) A free two-week 'debit P&L audit' from the FI's own statements: unit cost, network fees, incentives, routing. (2) A multi-network contingency pack so the FI can enable alternates (Pulse, NYCE, Visa Interlink/Plus, Mastercard Maestro/Cirrus, SHAZAM, CO-OP, Culiance, from memory) if an owner changes. (3) Open-book processing at disclosed cost plus a fixed fee. (4) Optional cooperative route for FIs that want equity in a routing layer.
ideas.why_now: The sale talks are live, Fiserv is pruning (ATM JV with Bridgeport, student loans sold), and processing contracts renewing in the next 24 months will be signed against that uncertainty.
ideas.wedge: The free audit sold to 30 FIs whose card contracts are up for renewal; ten convert to processing at their next contract.
ideas.path_to_100m: 29.84B exempt non-prepaid transactions a year (Fed 2023). At an assumed $0.035 net processing and routing margin a transaction, $100M is 2.86B transactions, 9.6% of the exempt pool; a small per-card fee brings it to about 6-8%. If the cooperative layer takes an Accel-sized routing business instead (single-message networks carried 28.84B transactions across all issuers; at a 5-10% share and $0.03-0.05 net a transaction that is $43-145M, share unverified), the path is shorter but needs a seller and capital. About 8% share is heroic but not absurd.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Fiserv (owns STAR and Accel), FIS (NYCE), Jack Henry, Elan, CO-OP, SHAZAM, Global Payments/TSYS issuer processing (all from memory); fintech-grade processors (Marqeta, Lithic, Highnote, Galileo, i2c, Thredd, from memory) serve fintechs, not community FIs.
ideas.why_they_lose: Each incumbent is conflicted: it owns or earns from a network, bundles processing into the core, and profits from opacity. Fintech-grade processors lack core integrations, ATM/PIN networks, dispute workflows and the FI sales motion. A potential megabank owner competes with the FIs it would serve.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning (open book), scale economies in processing, and cooperative equity that binds owner-FIs.
ideas.earned_secret: A network's real asset is not its software. It is the set of issuers that have enabled it on their cards. Issuers choose which networks are enabled, so together they hold the option.
ideas.first_90_days: Offer the audit to 30 FIs; map which networks each is enabled for; build the alternate-routing playbook per processor; open talks with CO-OP, SHAZAM and Culiance as partners; track the sale news weekly. Legal check: Regulation II requires at least two unaffiliated networks per authentication type and bars issuer routing restrictions (from memory); a joint decision by FIs to disable a network could look like a group boycott, so each FI must decide for itself and the cooperative must be a product, not an agreement.

ideas.title: Bureau
ideas.one_liner: Buy the independent bank and CU processors, and the pieces Fiserv wants to shed, whose 7-10-year contracts and high retention are the asset; consolidate them on one AI-run stack; run them at the incumbents' margin.
ideas.customer: The processors' owners (sellers) and the 100-300 FI clients each serves.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The FIs already pay. Buyer-side signer is the sponsor's investment committee with a lender; sellers are founders, families or small boards.
ideas.problem: The big three earn high margins from lock-in (Fiserv Financial Solutions is $9.7B of revenue). Independents lack scale and, I assume, run 10-20% margins. Strategic buyers are distracted or constrained, owners are ageing, and Fiserv is now selling: ATM and cash businesses into a JV with Bridgeport Partners (Fiserv keeps 49%), student-loan servicing to Infinite Computer Solutions, with 'other deals could follow'.
ideas.solution: Acquire four to six processors over three years; migrate each to a single multi-tenant stack using the Parity engine; automate support and regulatory updates; cross-sell digital banking, cards (Switchboard) and fraud tools; use Fiserv carve-outs as a supply of assets.
ideas.why_now: Supply of sellers is rising and AI lowers cost-to-serve. Against it: if the 10-year yield really is 5.35% (single secondary source, unverified), leverage is expensive.
ideas.wedge: First targets from the Kansas City Fed data: CSI (7% of banks), COCC (3%), Finastra's US business (3%); among CUs FedComp (about 10% in 2020), CompuSource, FLEX, Sharetec; plus DCI (core processor for community banks, FIntegrate's partner). Begin with the smallest (under $30M revenue) where an owner wants out.
ideas.path_to_100m: Independents' pool: about 13% of 4,450 banks (580 x $0.7M) plus about 20% of 4,214 CUs (840 x $0.3M) = about $0.4B + $0.25B = $0.65B (shares from Kansas City Fed and Credit Union Times, revenue per FI assumed). $100M of revenue is about 15% of that pool: four to six acquisitions of $15-40M revenue each. At 2-3x revenue the capital needed is $200-300M (assumed). Share is heroic, but it is bought rather than won, so the constraint is capital and integration skill, not a model lead.
ideas.who_does_it_today: PE-owned CSI (taken private in 2022, from memory); Candescent (ex-NCR digital banking, Veritas, from memory); Bridgeport Partners (took the MoneyPass JV) and Infinite Computer Solutions (took student-loan servicing); Jack Henry and Fiserv as bolt-on buyers; Constellation-style software consolidators (from memory).
ideas.why_they_lose: PE owners usually buy for quick margin through price rises and cost cuts, which triggers the churn that contract lock-in holds back. Strategics are distracted and face antitrust and exam scrutiny. Co-operative owners cannot raise acquisition capital.
ideas.moat: Scale economies (shared data centre, support and regulatory-update engineering), switching costs (the contracts), cornered resource (deal flow from retiring founders and Fiserv carve-outs).
ideas.earned_secret: The lock-in that makes Fiserv rich also sits inside a small processor's contracts, which is why these businesses are financeable. They are cheap because they are sub-scale, not because the revenue is weak.
ideas.first_90_days: Build the target list from Kansas City Fed and ABA data; approach five owners with under $40M of revenue; line up a sponsor and a lender; draft the 100-day consolidation plan on the Parity engine. Legal check: change-of-control and assignment consents in client contracts, client banks' third-party diligence on a new owner, regulators' examination of technology service providers; none looks blocking but consent mechanics decide timing and price.

ideas.title: Gap Ledger
ideas.one_liner: A cap-gap ledger for graduate deans that shows each admitted student's remaining federal headroom and the exact buydown dollars needed to keep them, then lets the school buy one fixed per-loan fee for a program-wide fixed rate from a competing lender panel.
ideas.customer: Graduate and professional programs priced above the new caps: MBA (non-professional tier, $20,500 a year), law, medicine, dentistry, veterinary and pharmacy (professional tier, hitting the $200,000 aggregate), later doctoral health programs; extension to the Parent PLUS cap for undergraduate-serving institutions.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The school's institutional aid / discount budget plus the enrollment-software line. Signer: associate dean for admissions and aid, with the school CFO signing off on accounting treatment.
ideas.problem: No one holds one number per admit. Headroom depends on the tier, part-time proration, grandfathering, a $257,500 lifetime cap and a professional-degree list that ED changed on 29 Jun and 10 Jul under a court stay. NBER calls the legal and admin cost of buydown and risk-share deals 'non-trivial', and lenders must negotiate across thousands of institutions. A school guarantee lands on the CFO as a contingent liability [M: ASC 460]; a fixed per-loan fee is a known cost. Harvard's own summary says only a few lenders offered a competitive fixed rate to all students regardless of credit.
ideas.solution: Step 1: a ledger fed by SIS/CRM data, a mapping of ED's list to CIP codes and student-consented NSLDS data, producing a gap per admit by week. Step 2: a points desk where the school sets a capped fee per funded loan, uses a standard contract and runs an annual rate-card process among at least three unaffiliated lenders (HEOA), with tail risk placed with the Seasoning Factory.
ideas.why_now: The caps took effect 1 Jul 2026; the first full admit cycle under them runs November to January; about 80% of dentistry and 62% of medical borrowers exceed their cap; the professional list is in flux; Harvard and others are now running formal lender processes with risk-share language.
ideas.wedge: Law schools and MBA programs outside the top 20 (lenders chase the steep-earnings top programs first). First 10: programs whose aid offices run a lender RFP this winter. No signed customers; none claimed.
ideas.path_to_100m: Leg 1, software: ~1,000 programs (law, MBA, medicine, dental, vet, pharmacy, doctoral health) x $50k = $50M, which is most of that universe, so heroic alone. Leg 2, the desk: schools buy buydowns on ~$2B/yr of loans at 4 points = $80M/yr of school fees, of which we keep ~15% = $12M, plus interest on any paper we hold ($1.0B at 10% = $100M, via the Seasoning Factory). Parent PLUS extension adds institutions. Honest read: software alone tops out near $50M; $100M needs the desk plus a held book.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Ascent Funding (rated school risk-share, 100+ graduate partners, 2,300+ institutions, $45M Series C Feb 2026); Sallie Mae / SoFi / Citizens school programs; Juno (student side, claims 14-15% of private in-school graduate lending); SIS vendors (Ellucian, Workday, Anthology) that will ship cap logic [M]; enrollment consultancies (RNL, EAB) on the undergraduate side [M].
ideas.why_they_lose: Ascent and every lender are conflicted sellers, and HEOA forces schools to list at least three unaffiliated lenders, so a lender-owned tool cannot be the school's agent. SIS vendors ship compliance logic, not pricing, RFPs or contracts. Juno works for students. Nobody is the school's neutral buyer-side agent.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (the ledger becomes the record of aid-gap data) and counter-positioning against lender-owned tools.
ideas.earned_secret: Aid directors do not need more lender options; they need one number, the cost to keep each admit. A fixed, capped per-loan fee fits the discount budget; a guarantee does not fit the CFO.
ideas.first_90_days: Build the ledger for three programs from live admit data; map GENERAL-26-42 to CIP codes; draft a standard buydown contract and a three-lender RFP; run one RFP for one law school; get one CFO's written accounting view.

ideas.title: Seasoning Factory
ideas.one_liner: A bank-partnered, on-balance-sheet buyer of outcome-based graduate loans from many small originators on one tape standard, funded by insurer term notes and a first-loss slice, that builds the performance record ABS investors say they need.
ideas.customer: Originators that can underwrite but cannot fund (Ascent-type risk-share lenders, second-look lenders, credit-union service organizations, state authorities) and the insurers and asset-based-finance desks that want student-loan collateral beyond Sallie Mae.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Originators pay through the loan price (they sell at an agreed discount or premium). Capital comes from an insurer CIO or an ABF head. Signers: originator CFO/treasurer and the capital partner's investment committee.
ideas.problem: NBER's capital constraint: 100% bank risk weight (~10.5% capital), student-loan ABS of only $6.5-9.3B a year that mostly refinances, and a chicken-and-egg on data (investors need performance data on the specific underwriting model; lenders can only generate it at scale). The paper calls the fix (standard reporting, pilots, early credit enhancement) 'undefined'. Sallie Mae solved its own problem with KKR (min $2B a year of new loans), which leaves smaller originators without a buyer.
ideas.solution: The Factory is the buyer: standard tape and chain-of-title custody; forward-flow from 8-10 originators; insurer term notes matched to a 10-15 year asset; a first-loss slice (equity plus originator and school retained pieces); quarterly program-level performance reporting; later seasoned pools go to public or 144A ABS. Program-level price differences live in the purchase grid (an investor choice), not in the originator's credit decision, which is a legal premise needing counsel under Reg B and state law.
ideas.why_now: The private graduate market must grow 6-7x in about 12 months; CFPB's Reg B rule (effective 21 Jul 2026) removed the federal disparate-impact test; KKR's deal shows ABF desks pay for flow; Discover's $10.1B and Wells Fargo's $10B exits left Carlyle/KKR and Apollo/Blackstone with ~$20B of legacy loans and no origination.
ideas.wedge: Forward-flow for school-sponsored risk-share loans and second-look loans, with a 10% first-loss slice. Targets (not customers): Ascent-like lenders, second-look lenders, two or three CUSOs, one or two state authorities, two insurers.
ideas.path_to_100m: ~$300M a year of purchases for four years builds a $1.0B balance; at an assumed 10% gross yield that is $100M of consolidated interest revenue from ~3.2% of the $9.4B market ($8B gap + $1.4B existing). Capital: ~$100-120M equity and first loss plus ~$0.9B of term notes. Revenue, not profit: the profit is the excess spread after 6-7% funding and losses.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Sallie Mae-KKR (vertical, own loans only); SoFi, Earnest and College Ave securitizing their own books; Carlyle/KKR and Apollo/Blackstone holding legacy books; Nelnet's Firstmark servicing. I found no multi-originator student-loan aggregator. First Marblehead is the dead precedent.
ideas.why_they_lose: Sallie Mae buys only its own loans. ABF desks buy finished portfolios, not new programs from many small originators. Banks cannot hold at 10.5% capital. Small originators cannot produce investor-grade data alone.
ideas.moat: Scale economies (cost of funds) and a cornered resource (the one pooled, standard loan-level dataset on outcome-based graduate loans); switching costs for originators (tape and custody).
ideas.earned_secret: Investors price the first-loss holder and the document chain, not the borrower. First Marblehead died on both: guarantor TERI was downgraded in March 2008 and had to post cash, and its trusts later could not prove who owned the loans (>$5B uncollectable per court filings). Do it with no single guarantor and with custody from day one.
ideas.first_90_days: Counsel memo on secondary-grid pricing under Reg B and state law; letters of intent from three originators on tape standards; a $25M pilot through a bank partner; one insurer sizes a $250M delayed-draw note; trustee custody set up.

ideas.title: Offer-Backed
ideas.one_liner: In-school graduate loans for clinicians underwritten on a hospital's no-clawback hiring commitment, repaid first from the paycheck and priced off the hospital's credit, paid for out of the contingent-labor budget the hospital would otherwise give to staffing agencies.
ideas.customer: Health systems and large community hospitals hiring nurse practitioners, nurse anesthetists, PAs, physical and occupational therapists and pharmacists, and the students in those programs.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Health-system CFO with the CNO or chief people officer. Budget lines: contingent labor (SIA 2025: travel nurse $15.8B, allied $9.9B, locum $9.6B, per diem $5.2B), sign-on and retention bonuses, and the $5,250 IRC section 127 tuition/loan benefit.
ideas.problem: Employers already pay, but late: Clasp's customers have allocated over $130M; Rochester Regional offers up to $180K per nurse anesthetist and Allegheny Health Network up to $110K. That money repays loans after hire. In school the student still borrows at 10-17%, and the hospital cannot guarantee the loan without a stay-or-pay claim (CA AB 692 in force since 1 Jan 2026; NY Trapped at Work Act, reportedly effective Dec 2026).
ideas.solution: The hospital signs a non-binding commitment with no clawback and pays the lender a monthly section 127 benefit for each month the clinician is employed, plus a one-time program fee at hire. The student signs a loan; once employed, a voluntary, revocable direct-deposit split (Pinwheel/Truv/Argyle-type plumbing) sends a share of pay to the lender first. The lender prices off the offer and the hospital's pledge. Carrot-only design fits AB 692 and the New York carve-out.
ideas.why_now: Caps in force; the court stay may lift (which would restore much of the PT/nursing gap); AB 692 and New York remove the stick; section 127 student-loan repayment is now permanent; Clasp's $20M Series B (Jan 2026) shows employers are buying the repayment half.
ideas.wedge: Private nurse-anesthesia, DNP and physical-therapy programs (high price, high employer demand). First 10: health systems that already allocate loan-repayment budgets; Clasp's published customers (Boston Children's, UMass Memorial, UNC Health Appalachian, OhioHealth) show the type of buyer, not my customers.
ideas.path_to_100m: ~9,200 financed students a year x $38k = ~$350M/yr, about 7-8% of ~120,000 annual completers in hospital-relevant clinical graduate programs (my rough sum, unsourced). A 3-4 year ramp builds a ~$1.0B balance; at 8.5% (hospital-credit pricing) that is $85M of interest, plus a $5,000 program fee on ~8,000 hires = $40M, total ~$125M. Hospital spend is ~$21k per student, ~$190M per annual cohort, ~0.5% of ~$39B staffing spend. If the stay lifts, NBER's field figures (PT $3.2B, nursing $2.9B) make the pool much larger; if it holds, this is a pricing and pipeline product for programs above $50k a year.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Clasp (repayment side, $20M B, >$130M allocated, no in-school lending reported); employer tuition-for-commitment programs (e.g., Rush nurse anesthesia); Sallie Mae/SoFi/College Ave in-school loans; tuition-benefit platforms [M: Guild, InStride]; staffing agencies (Aya 16.3% share, CHG 7.4%).
ideas.why_they_lose: Clasp is software with no balance sheet or lender. Lenders cannot underwrite an employer's promise. Staffing agencies profit from the shortage and cannot sell its cure. Hospital treasuries cannot hold consumer loans.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (pooled, rated employer commitments), switching costs (payroll and benefit integrations), counter-positioning against staffing agencies.
ideas.earned_secret: The cheapest credit in the clinician pipeline is the future employer's balance sheet, but it sits in HR's recruiting budget, not in Treasury. A no-clawback pledge is legal in every state and still moves the rate.
ideas.first_90_days: Counsel memo on AB 692, New York, section 127 and whether a pooled arrangement is an ERISA plan or insurance product; term sheet with one bank or credit-union partner; three health systems and two nurse-anesthesia or DNP programs; pilot 50 students.

ideas.title: Operator Rail
ideas.one_liner: Sell graduate financing to the few operators that run most cap-exposed online and health-professions programs, fund it as a per-start conversion fee from their marketing budgets, and become the lender of record behind their programs.
ideas.customer: Multi-brand operators and OPM-run portfolios. Adtalem alone reports 97,359 students (Sep 2025) across Chamberlain, Walden, and the Ross and AUC medical schools, with ~$1.95B fiscal-2026 revenue (secondary). Others on my [M] list, not sized: Grand Canyon, Strategic Education/Capella, Touro, Risepoint, Noodle.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The operator's student-acquisition budget (marketing and recruitment), paid per funded start. Signer: CFO with the chief enrollment officer.
ideas.problem: The caps hit the operators' highest-priced programs. Operators hold the funnel data, call centers and clinical-site networks but sell through whatever lender panel each brand has. Enrollment-to-start conversion is their P&L line, and a financing failure is a lost acquisition cost [M: my insider hypothesis, no conversion data found].
ideas.solution: One operator-wide rate card for every student in its programs, paid as a per-start fee rather than a guarantee, with the tail placed with a third party (Seasoning Factory) so the operator is not the guarantor. For proprietary operators, 90/10 matters: private loans count as non-Title IV, but treatment of a school guarantee is unresolved, so the design avoids one.
ideas.why_now: Caps took effect 1 Jul 2026; Adtalem's growth is uneven (Walden +13.6%, Chamberlain +2.2% in Q1 FY26) and analysts flag its graduate exposure.
ideas.wedge: Graduate nursing and health programs at ground-based operators; the first deal is one brand of one operator.
ideas.path_to_100m: ~16,000 funded students a year x $22k = ~$350M/yr; four years builds a ~$1.0B balance (10% yield = $100M). If 35% of graduate starts are above the cap and we fund 65% of those (my assumptions), that needs ~70,000 graduate starts a year at the anchor operators, which I cannot show (Adtalem's 97,359 includes undergraduates). Heroic unless the operator set is wider than five; rests on 3-4 anchor contracts.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Ascent (works with schools of all kinds); Sallie Mae, SoFi and MPOWER through operators' own lender panels; Climb for career training.
ideas.why_they_lose: Lenders sell school by school. A lender willing to be the operator-wide program lender, with risk transferred, gets tens of thousands of loans from three or four signatures.
ideas.moat: Switching costs and a cornered resource (operator contracts and funnel data).
ideas.earned_secret: Operators already pay a conversion price (acquisition cost per start). A financing fee is cheaper per start than another lead, and it is the only lever they control after the application.
ideas.first_90_days: Read 34 CFR 668.28 and Appendix C with a lawyer; model one operator's last two years of starts against the cap; draft the per-start fee agreement; get an introduction to one operator's treasurer.

ideas.title: Program Score Exchange
ideas.one_liner: A neutral exchange where lenders contribute loan performance tapes and schools contribute consented alumni earnings, and ABS investors, rating agencies, schools and lenders buy program-level scores no single lender can publish; the 'FICO for programs' NBER says is missing.
ideas.customer: ABS investors and rating agencies, ABF desks, lenders, and ~1,500 graduate-serving schools.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Investor data budgets, lender risk and analytics budgets, school institutional-research budgets. Signers: chief risk officer, head of structured finance, vice provost.
ideas.problem: NBER says the lack of 'an industry-standard scoring framework' analogous to FICO limits scale and capital. Structural dilemma: lenders cannot publish program-level prices (state-AG exposure; Earnest paid MA AG $2.5M) or easily pool data; ED publishes backward-looking Scorecard data, not forward scores; rating agencies rate institutions, not programs [M]; schools cannot grade themselves.
ideas.solution: Standard loan-level reporting in exchange for benchmarking. Program-level scores used by investors (purchase grids, reserves), schools (sizing a reserve or buydown) and lenders (loss reserves, pool selection), with documented business-necessity and less-discriminatory-alternative analysis for lenders that choose to use it in underwriting.
ideas.why_now: Reg B dropped the federal effects test on 21 Jul 2026; the market must grow 6-7x; the earnings test gives every program an official earnings label from 2027.
ideas.wedge: Benchmarking for lenders that fund school-sponsored programs, sold alongside the Seasoning Factory's data. First 10: five lenders and three ABF desks.
ideas.path_to_100m: Rating agencies and investors: 5 x $1.5M + 30 x $0.5M = $22M. Lenders: 40 x $0.4M = $16M. Schools: 1,500 x $30k = $45M. Per-score fees: 3M applications x $3 = $9M. Total ~$92M at near-full adoption. Heroic; needs the earnings data from the Earnings Replica as a second source.
ideas.who_does_it_today: College Scorecard and PEER (free; earnings data for only ~12,700 of ~41,000 matched programs), Lightcast, Gray, Ascent's proprietary outcomes model, FICO and the bureaus (individual-level only).
ideas.why_they_lose: Free federal data is backward-looking and, per one analyst, stale (earnings not updated past 2019-20); lenders' models are proprietary and legally exposed; bureaus score people, not programs.
ideas.moat: Network economies (more lenders, more tapes, better scores) and a cornered resource (pooled loan performance by program).
ideas.earned_secret: A score that no lender uses to decide individual credit, and that investors and schools use to price risk, keeps the exposure where the law is weakest.
ideas.first_90_days: Counsel memo on FCRA and Reg B status of a program-level score; sign three lenders to a reporting pilot; draft the tape standard with a rating agency.

ideas.title: Employer-Cohort Cap-Fit
ideas.one_liner: Graduate programs priced at or under the $20,500 federal annual limit so no private debt is needed, recruited through hospital and district employers instead of paid marketing, with the university granting the degree and the platform running curriculum, clinical placement and cohorts for a fee.
ideas.customer: Universities with spare graduate capacity, and health systems and school districts with cohorts of 20-50 employees (RN-to-MSN, MSW, school counseling, special-education licensure).
ideas.payer_and_signer: The university pays a services fee from tuition; the employer pays tuition or cohort fees from its pipeline budget. Signers: provost or dean, and the health system's CNO or chief people officer.
ideas.problem: The OPM model needs a $40-60k price to fund marketing and a 40-60% revenue share. 2U filed Chapter 11 in July 2024 and Wiley's OPM unit was sold to Academic Partnerships (now Risepoint) for $150M; colleges are pulling programs in-house, Minnesota barred tuition-share contracts at public colleges, and incentive-compensation rules cloud revenue share. The caps make $20,500 the price at which a non-professional master's needs no private loan.
ideas.solution: A flat fee for design, delivery support, clinical placement and cohort management, with the performance part tied to persistence and completion (not recruitment). Enrollment comes from employer channels with near-zero acquisition cost.
ideas.why_now: The price anchor is new, the OPM model is broken at that price, and employers have pipeline budgets (see Offer-Backed).
ideas.wedge: RN-to-MSN and school-counseling cohorts at three regional universities with one health system or district partner each.
ideas.path_to_100m: At 17% of $20,500 = $3,500 per student-year, $100M needs ~28,600 enrolled students, ~0.9% of ~3.1M graduate students [M], i.e., 100+ programs. Honest read: this sits where the OPM industry has been losing, and Guild and InStride already sell employer-funded degrees.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Guild, InStride (Strategic Education), Coursera degrees, Risepoint, Noodle, Georgia Tech's low-cost master's and other public online programs [M].
ideas.why_they_lose: OPMs cannot serve a $20,500 price with paid marketing. Universities have no employer channel. Employers cannot grant degrees.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (employer cohort relationships) and process power (clinical placement operations).
ideas.earned_secret: The expensive part of a graduate program is finding the student. If the employer sends the student, a price at the cap works.
ideas.first_90_days: Sign one health system and one regional university for a 30-student RN-to-MSN cohort priced under $41k; get counsel on a fee structure compliant with incentive-compensation rules; price clinical placement cost per student.

ideas.title: Earnings Replica
ideas.one_liner: For each graduate program, an alumni-consented replica of ED's earnings test built from tax transcripts and payroll data 12-18 months before ED's own determination, with student warnings and program-restructuring support.
ideas.customer: Graduate-serving institutions, especially those with master's programs in counseling, social work, education, arts and humanities; later every program (the test also covers undergraduate programs).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Provost or CFO; budget: institutional research and compliance. The consequence is statutory: a failing program must warn students, and a second failure in three years costs Direct Loans for at least two years.
ideas.problem: ED's determinations go out in early 2027 and appeals are limited to ED's calculation. Public data is stale (one analyst says Scorecard earnings have not been updated past 2019-20) and schools cannot see IRS earnings, so the schools with no data find out last.
ideas.solution: Alumni opt in through the school to share tax transcripts or payroll data. We compute ED's median-vs-bachelor's test by program, report an early determination and margin, generate the student warning and benchmark restructuring options.
ideas.why_now: Determinations early 2027; first applicable award year 2027-28; first possible loss of Direct Loans in award year 2028-29; one report of ED's analysis has 4% of graduate programs failing, with mental and social health services (including counseling) the one large field where most fall below the benchmark.
ideas.wedge: Master's programs in mental and social health services and education at mid-size private and regional public universities. First 10: schools that already survey alumni salaries.
ideas.path_to_100m: ~1,200 graduate-serving institutions x $50k = $60M, plus ~1,500 institutions with undergraduate and certificate programs x $30k = $45M (the test covers every program): ~$105M at ~2,700 institutions. Heroic (near saturation) and SIS vendors and EAB will bundle; the exchange's lender/investor data adds the other side.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Prentus (outcome tracking), Anthology, bank advisory blogs (UMB), Lightcast, Gray, EAB [S]. ED's own determination is free.
ideas.why_they_lose: They model from public data that is years stale or from self-reported pay. A replica from consented transcripts is the only forward-looking, program-level view of the data ED will use.
ideas.moat: Cornered resource (consented alumni earnings by program) and switching costs once alumni data is connected.
ideas.earned_secret: Schools hold what ED does not: alumni who will answer a request. Consented transcripts turn that relationship into a 12-month head start.
ideas.first_90_days: Run a consent pilot with 300 alumni at two schools; reproduce the test on a public subset to check method; get counsel on the transcript consent mechanism ([M] IRS Form 4506-C through an IVES participant, or payroll APIs) and FERPA.

ideas.title: Verified-Pay Part-Timer
ideas.one_liner: Graduate loans for working adults employed in their field, underwritten on verified payroll and repaid first through a voluntary direct-deposit split, with in-school interest paid from salary so balances do not capitalize.
ideas.customer: Part-time graduate students with jobs (RN to NP, teacher to counselor, analyst to MBA), many of whom hit prorated federal limits.
ideas.payer_and_signer: The borrower signs; some employers contribute through tuition benefits (section 127, up to $5,250 a year tax-free).
ideas.problem: NBER's footnote: part-time students, including those continuing from before July 2026, get lower limits based on enrollment intensity. Lenders underwrite on score and cosigner, and the paper says program-level data is legally exposed. Individual verified income is the clean alternative, and payroll-linked repayment is already proven in personal loans.
ideas.solution: Income verified by payroll connection, a loan sized to net pay, a payroll split (fixed dollars or share of net pay), and in-school interest-only paid from salary. No program-level data in pricing, so the product does not depend on the Reg B outcome.
ideas.why_now: Proration is new in 2026; payroll-connectivity vendors (Pinwheel, Truv, Argyle) exist; section 127 lets some employers add a tax-free contribution.
ideas.wedge: RN-to-MSN and DNP students employed at one health system; teacher-to-counselor students employed at one district. First 10: employers that run a tuition benefit and will host the payroll connection.
ideas.path_to_100m: If 20% of the 370,000 displaced borrowers are working part-timers (my assumption) = 74,000 x $21.6k = ~$1.6B a year. A 20% share = ~$320M a year, which builds a $1.0B balance in about four years; at 9-10% that is $90-100M.
ideas.who_does_it_today: SoFi and Earnest (income and cash-flow underwriting), Funding U (individual academic performance), payroll-linked lenders such as Kashable and Highline for personal loans, Sallie Mae with a cosigner.
ideas.why_they_lose: Banks must underwrite ability to repay the highest amortizing payment (OCC Bulletin 2015-7) and securitize fixed cash flows, so they stay on score and cosigner. Payroll-connectivity vendors do not lend. Nobody sells both to the part-time graduate student.
ideas.moat: Switching costs (payroll connection) and cheaper capital as loss data accumulates.
ideas.earned_secret: Collection priority can matter as much as score: a borrower who has chosen to route pay to the lender first is a different credit than the same borrower on autopay.
ideas.first_90_days: Counsel memo on revocable payroll splits, state wage-assignment law and UDAAP risk; a bank partner; 100 loans at one health system; measure delinquency against a control.

ideas.title: The Meter: client-owned proof of what offshore vendors actually delivered
ideas.one_liner: A vendor-neutral system, owned by the client, that reads logs the client already holds (logins, tickets, commits, AI-gateway calls, invoices) to prove what offshore engineers delivered, clause by clause, and is paid mostly out of the savings it proves.
ideas.customer: US enterprises spending $20M+ a year on outsourced application, testing and infrastructure services (about 1,500 firms, roughly $70B of the $100B pool; my estimate). Start with banks, insurers and payers with a contract renewing within 12 months.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Chief Procurement Officer or VP IT Sourcing signs; CIO and CISO approve read-only telemetry. Budget: a contingent 15-25% of verified recoveries and price cuts (no new budget needed) plus a $150-400k/yr subscription from the vendor-governance line (ISG just signed a governance contract worth up to $17M with one manufacturer, so the line exists).
ideas.problem: The baseline in nearly every master agreement is FTEs, not work. The vendor holds the only evidence of how much was done by people versus AI, while about 25% of contracts are renegotiated each year (Cognizant CFO), clients want 25-30% cuts (Persistent CEO), and AI pass-through clauses are spreading (Cognizant-Daimler Truck). Advisers (ISG about $250M/yr revenue, Gartner, Everest) are paid per deal and also sell to vendors. Service credits go unpaid because earn-back clauses cancel them (Forrester).
ideas.solution: Read-only connectors to client-owned systems where vendor staff work: IdP/VPN/VDI logs, Git/CI, Jira/ServiceNow, the client's LLM gateway, AP and SOW data. Outputs: invoice-to-activity reconciliation (ghost and double-billed FTEs), unit cost per ticket/PR/change request with AI-adjusted should-cost, a clause engine (productivity glide paths, escalator caps, benchmarking rights, AI pass-through formulas), renegotiation/rebid packs, and a signed AI-gain ledger that makes the Meter the neutral calculation agent for gain-share deals. Forward-deployed staff are ex-vendor delivery heads (top-5 Indian firms' headcount fell 7,389 in FY26; TCS cut about 12,000 mostly mid/senior roles).
ideas.why_now: 25%-a-year renegotiation rate; AI clauses in new deals; many client policies ban vendor GenAI use without consent and cannot verify compliance (Morgan Lewis); Section 174A (foreign software R&E amortized over 15 years, permanent law even though the $100K H-1B fee was vacated in June 2026) gives a VP of Tax a reason to want location-attested activity logs.
ideas.wedge: A 90-day ghost-FTE and unexercised-rights audit on one $30M+/yr contract renewing within 12 months, sold on contingency. First 10: Fortune-1000 banks, insurers and payers whose CPO already hired an adviser for a rebid, reached via ex-ISG/Everest consultants and PE operating partners.
ideas.path_to_100m: About 1,500 targets at roughly $47M average offshore spend (my estimate). Verified savings plus recoveries of 4-6%/yr (floor: an outsourcing consultant says line-item review yields at least 1% of contract value per unchecked year; BlueOptima claims up to 20%, vendor claim). At 4% savings and 20% fee plus $200k subscription: about $573k per client, 174 clients (11.6% of 1,500). At 6% and 25%: about $900k, 111 clients (7.4%). No step needs more than 12% share.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Advisers: ISG, Gartner, Everest, HFS. Vendor-output measurement: BlueOptima (code-effort benchmarking since about 2009; a directory lists about 109 staff, unverified). Internal-team analytics: Jellyfish, Faros, DX (Atlassian agreed to buy for about $1B). Generic recovery audit: PRGX (has an IT contract labor case study), Vaudit. Contingent-labor systems: SAP Fieldglass, Beeline. Secure third-party access: Island ($6.4B valuation, about $200M ARR). In-house VMOs with spreadsheets.
ideas.why_they_lose: Advisers cannot sell continuous measurement without cutting their per-deal model. Engineering analytics sells to engineering leaders about their own teams, not to procurement with clause logic. BlueOptima has measured code for 15 years without becoming a procurement standard because buyers lacked a forcing event; renegotiation plus AI clauses now supplies one. Vendors cannot audit themselves.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning against advisers and vendors whose revenue depends on opacity; cornered resource in a cross-client database of ticket- and PR-level unit prices vendors never publish; switching costs once the Meter is the named calculation agent in the contract.
ideas.earned_secret: The client owns the system of record where vendor staff work, while the vendor owns the invoice, and nobody joins the two. Most master agreements carry a 3-5% annual productivity glide path that has never been audited because the baseline was frozen in FTEs, not work units (background knowledge from sourcing practice; the first deliverable tests it).
ideas.first_90_days: Sign 3 design partners with renewals inside 12 months; build 4 connectors (Entra/Okta+VPN logs, Jira/ServiceNow, GitHub/GitLab/ADO, AP/SOW exports); run one ghost-FTE reconciliation and one contract-rights-not-exercised report; hire 2 ex-vendor delivery heads. Legal checks: audit/telemetry rights in the MSA, India DPDP and employee-monitoring consent, vendor flow-down notice.

ideas.title: Penny-Exact: independent proof that the AI-translated system behaves identically
ideas.one_liner: An independent referee that proves, to the penny, that an AI-translated mainframe or legacy system behaves exactly like the old one, and issues evidence an auditor, regulator and board will accept.
ideas.customer: Banks, insurers, payers and government agencies running material COBOL/PL/I/DB2 batch estates that start modernization within 12 months; then any enterprise running an AI-assisted migration (Oracle Forms, PL/SQL to Postgres, Informatica, Teradata, Java/.NET upgrades, SAP custom code).
ideas.payer_and_signer: Program CIO or COO signs; Chief Audit Executive (and in banks the CRO) must accept the evidence. Budget: the testing and acceptance line of the modernization program (a modernization vendor models UAT sign-off, parallel running, regulatory approval and acceptance testing as the roughly 62% of effort AI leaves untouched). Modernization vendors are a second payer because acceptance gates their final invoice.
ideas.problem: Translation is becoming free: AWS Transform converts COBOL to Java in months, and Anthropic's 2026-02-23 post knocked IBM down about 13% in a day (IBM Z revenue still grew 48% the prior quarter). What remains is proving the new system matches the old on 30 years of edge cases (rounding, packed decimals, EBCDIC collation, date windowing, sort stability, abend/restart, batch order). Whoever sells the translation also sells its own proof.
ideas.solution: Read-only taps on production inputs/outputs (batch files, DB2 snapshots, CICS/MQ traces) produce golden datasets; old and new run in shadow on the same inputs; an AI classifier sorts differences into intended changes and defects. Product: an Equivalence Certificate per application and cutover wave, signed by the referee and backed by the stored golden record (a lasting test oracle). Priced per wave plus platform licence plus 12 months of post-cutover monitoring.
ideas.why_now: The translation shock just happened (AWS launch May 2025; Anthropic post Feb 2026). Boards that watched IBM fall are asking for exit cases, and sign-off now sits on the critical path.
ideas.wedge: Ten insurers and regional banks ($5-50B assets/premiums) with COBOL batch suites, a modernization starting within 12 months and no integrator locked in. Second channel: AWS Transform and other translation partners wanting a neutral acceptance layer to unlock their final milestone.
ideas.path_to_100m: Mainframe: about 35 programs/yr at roughly $1.2M each (12-15% of a roughly $9M testing/acceptance line in a $25M program) = about $42M. Other AI-assisted migrations: about 150 programs/yr at roughly $400k = about $60M. Total about $100M at roughly 185 programs/yr. Borderline: needs about 10-15% of AI-assisted migration programs in mid/large enterprises; the program count is my estimate and could not be sourced.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Mechanical Orchard (Series A $24M; Imogen captures production behavior and claims continuous equivalence, but inside its own migration); AWS Transform; IBM watsonx tools and the large integrators (Accenture, TCS, Infosys, Cognizant), each validating its own work; Hypercubic ($5.3M seed, Aug 2026) and Kodesage ($6.6M seed) on legacy understanding/translation; Datafold for SQL/warehouse migrations; Tricentis/Parasoft test tools; Big 4 IV&V on large government programs.
ideas.why_they_lose: Translators grade their own homework and an audit committee knows it. Test tools generate tests but do not issue accepted evidence. Integrators bill time and materials for acceptance and have no reason to shorten it.
