ideas.moat: Neutral position (counter-positioning against every translator) that works like a rating agency or auditor, valuable once examiners and Big 4 audit partners accept the format (cornered resource); a library of per-language and per-platform gotcha test packs; process power from repeated cutovers.
ideas.earned_secret: Every failed cutover fails on a behavior nobody wrote down (a sort tie-break, a month-end-only rounding rule, a restart that reruns a half-posted file). Production data, not specifications, is the only complete spec, and it exists only in the system being replaced (background knowledge).
ideas.first_90_days: Build a replay harness around a z/OS batch emulator and a DB2 snapshot differ; partner with one integrator running AWS Transform and one mid-size insurer; run an equivalence report on one batch suite; show the certificate format to the insurer's internal auditor and a Big 4 audit partner. Legal: no US rule found that mandates independent equivalence certification, so demand is for defensible evidence; keep independence clean (never paid by the translator for the same program).

ideas.title: The Middle: a sponsor-level AI-native maintenance utility for PE portfolios
ideas.one_liner: A private-equity sponsor signs one framework agreement and every portfolio company gets fixed-unit-price AI-native application maintenance and development from a shared pod, below the big Indian firms' minimum ticket and clean to carve out at exit.
ideas.customer: PE-owned US companies with $50M-1B revenue. S&P Global counts 82,927 US private companies owned by PE (Aug 2025); I assume about 8,000 fall in this band (my estimate).
ideas.payer_and_signer: The sponsor's operating partner or head of portfolio operations signs the framework (value-creation-plan cost take-out is the budget line); each portfolio CIO or CFO issues work orders.
ideas.problem: A $200M-revenue portfolio company spends roughly 3-5% of revenue on IT (my estimate), a fifth on offshore-deliverable maintenance and development bought one company at a time from tier-2 vendors with no leverage and no standard security pack. The majors will not take sub-$5M tickets. Few sponsors built shared outsourcing, historically because it complicates exits; AlixPartners now says portfolio teams are warming to low-touch shared services and Zinnov says PE increasingly centralizes vendor management.
ideas.solution: A shared delivery utility with unit prices (per ticket resolved, per accepted story, per application-year), 40% below current tier-2 spend on common stacks (Salesforce, NetSuite, Dynamics, Workday, .NET, Java), a sponsor-level pre-approved security and data pack (30-day onboarding), 90-day exit rights and a portable runbook so a buyer at exit gets a clean data room. AI-native pods in India with a US account lead, measured by the Meter.
ideas.why_now: Cost take-out pressure with AI deflation visible (clients seek 25-30% cuts); the H-1B/onsite model is unreliable; delivery agents are good enough for common-stack maintenance with human oversight (Infosys announced a Devin-based hybrid-pod model in Jan 2026).
ideas.wedge: One mid-market sponsor with 25+ companies on overlapping stacks; first 10 customers are ten of its portfolio companies, starting with the most repeated cheap work (Salesforce/NetSuite administration and enhancements, tier-2 application support).
ideas.path_to_100m: About 8,000 companies x roughly $1.2M offshore-deliverable spend = about $9.6B pool (my estimate). $100M is 1.0% of the pool, about 83 companies, e.g. six sponsors with 14 companies each. Revenue is delivery revenue as principal, not a fee on spend.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Tier-2 Indian and US vendors and boutiques (Endava, Perficient, Slalom, Globant, EPAM at the upper end); PE-focused IT support firms; EY and Zinnov selling shared-service platforms as consulting (EY claims 50-60% five-year savings from labor arbitrage, plus 10-15% centralization and 12-18% automation; vendor claim); AI-native single-platform entrants (Tessera Labs, $60M Series A, SAP first; AppFactor, $4M seed).
ideas.why_they_lose: Tier-2 vendors have no sponsor-level standard and no incentive to ease exits. Consultancies sell a design, not the running service. AI-native startups sell one platform and one buyer at a time with long enterprise cycles; the sponsor channel compresses that.
ideas.moat: Scale economies on shared runbooks and prompts across a portfolio; switching costs inside each company; an exclusive sponsor framework (cornered distribution).
ideas.earned_secret: An operating partner can mandate a vendor across the whole portfolio within the first 100 days after a close and reports cost take-outs to investors; what stops them is fear of a tangled carve-out. Sell clean carve-out, not savings (background knowledge).
ideas.first_90_days: Sign one sponsor and three pilot companies; stand up a 40-person pod; get SOC 2 Type 1; publish the unit price card and exit-transfer runbook. Legal: portfolio-company data-protection agreements, each company contracts separately so the sponsor takes no liability.

ideas.title: Clawback: an IT-services contract recovery factory with claims financing
ideas.one_liner: A recovery-audit factory for IT-services contracts: find money vendors owe under rate cards, escalator caps, volume tiers, service-credit clauses and AI pass-through terms nobody enforces, take 20-30% of what comes back, and advance cash against signed credit memos.
ideas.customer: The same roughly 1,500 enterprises as the Meter, plus mid-market firms with $2-20M contracts that cannot afford a measurement project.
ideas.payer_and_signer: No budget line needed: the fee is contingent on recoveries, so the CFO or Controller signs with the CPO co-signing. This removes round 1's no-budget failure.
ideas.problem: Contracts leak after signature. An outsourcing consultant says line-item review yields at least 1% of contract value per unchecked year and about 5% of line items cannot be explained; a recovery vendor claims 3-7% (vendor claim); Forrester reports earn-back clauses mean many providers never pay service credits. Contingent recovery audit is a proven model (bids of 13.5-40% of recoveries; PRG-Schultz bid 20% flat in a 2004 state procurement).
ideas.solution: A rules library built for IT-services contracts (named-resource billing, FTE-to-ticket mismatches, volume tiers not applied, escalators above caps, benchmarking rights never used, service-credit earn-back traps, regulatory-change pass-through surcharges, duplicate and shared-resource billing). Look-backs on 24-36 months of invoices; recoveries land as credit memos; Clawback advances 50-70% of agreed credit memos from a credit facility and keeps the spread. A monitoring subscription bridges into the Meter.
ideas.why_now: Vendors fighting to hold revenue are more willing to settle legacy claims inside renegotiations (about 25% of contracts a year); AI-clause deals create new rights with no enforcement; any visa surcharge billed while the H-1B fee was in force and then vacated is a refund claim (a hypothesis to test, not a fact found).
ideas.wedge: Contracts renewed in the last 36 months that carry an escalator; look-backs on ten clients sourced through procurement-association members and PE operating partners.
ideas.path_to_100m: At 3% leakage of the $100B pool and a 25% fee the annual fee pool is $750M, so $100M needs 13%. At 1% leakage the pool is $250M and it needs 40% (fails); at 5% it is $1.25B and 8%. The idea works only if the first ten audits show at least 3% recoverable. No independent leakage study exists; the audits are the test.
ideas.who_does_it_today: PRGX (recovery audit; has an IT-contract-labor case study); Vaudit/VendorAudit (claims $1B+ of vendor spend audited); Cotiviti in healthcare; telecom-expense and freight-audit firms in adjacent categories; ISG and law firms at renewal; internal audit.
ideas.why_they_lose: Generic AP auditors lack IT-contract logic (FTE pools, resource units, earn-backs); advisers do not work on contingency for old invoices; neither can match a ticket to a login. Specialization is the only wedge and it is thin.
ideas.moat: Process power (a rules library that improves with every audit) and, with financing, a balance-sheet edge. Honest verdict: the weakest moat of the eight; its value is as the no-budget entry that funds the Meter.
ideas.earned_secret: Earn-back clauses let a provider avoid a credit by hitting a target for two consecutive months, so credits go unpaid even when quality is bad; the unpaid-credit pool is largest in contracts older than 24 months.
ideas.first_90_days: Run five contingency look-backs to measure the real recovery rate; build the rules library from them; set up a $10M receivables facility with a specialty lender; decide at day 90 whether the measured rate clears 3%.

ideas.title: Run-Base Shrinker: an energy-services company for the application estate
ideas.one_liner: We cut the run bill your offshore vendor is paid to maintain (repeat incidents, zombie applications, dead custom code), fund the engineering ourselves, and keep 30-50% of verified savings for three years.
ideas.customer: CIOs and CFOs of US enterprises with $20M+ of annual run spend with offshore application-management vendors; first wedge SAP ECC shops that have not yet released conversion budget.
ideas.payer_and_signer: CIO (budget owner) and CFO sign; Internal Audit signs the savings method. Budget: the run-cost line being reduced, so it is self-funding. The structure is the ESCO model: LBNL puts US ESCO revenue at $10.7B in 2024 (85% energy-savings performance contracts); no equivalent exists for IT run costs.
ideas.problem: Offshore maintenance is billed on volume (tickets, FTE pools, applications supported). The highest-return work, permanently fixing the few causes behind most tickets and deleting what nobody uses, shrinks the vendor's own revenue, so it sits in a problem-management clause and never gets done. Rimini Street argues publicly that time-and-materials structures have no provision for root-cause problem management. Zombie applications are common (an old CIO survey found about 15% underused).
ideas.solution: Four levers, each measured by the Meter: repeat-incident elimination (AI root cause, patch PR, regression, deploy); zombie application retirement from authentication and network logs with compliant read-only archives; dead custom code removal (first SAP custom Z objects before S/4 conversion; mainstream ECC maintenance is said to end 2027, not re-verified); licence and infrastructure right-sizing. Fees: 30-50% of audited run-cost reduction for 36 months; we fund the engineering.
ideas.why_now: AI makes root-cause fixes and code deletion cheap enough to fund on spec; clients demand 25-30% cuts; the SAP deadline gives CFOs a date; unit-priced and fixed-price deals pass reductions through. Contract check: volume bands and reduced-resource credits can leave a 20% ticket cut worth only 8-12% of fees unless the baseline resets, so target unit-priced or soon-to-renew contracts.
ideas.wedge: Ten SAP ECC enterprises: retire custom code before paying an integrator to convert it. Second wedge: zombie-application retirement for companies consolidating vendors.
ideas.path_to_100m: About $30M offshore run base per client x 12% reduction over 3 years x 35% share = $1.26M per client-year, so 79 clients (my estimates; the first audit tests the 12%). Pool view: if run-related offshore spend is about $40B, 12% is $4.8B/yr of savings and our 35% is $1.68B, so $100M is 6% of the shared-savings pool.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Rimini Street (third-party support for packaged software, about $430M revenue, background knowledge; sells cheaper support, not shared-savings shrink); the AMS vendors themselves (never); consultancy portfolio rationalization billed as projects (Deloitte, Accenture, TCS); app-retirement software (OpenText InfoArchive, Solix, Informatica; about $2.2B software market in 2025 per a vendor-style report); AI-native maintenance startups: AppFactor ($4M seed), LogicStar (pre-seed), DataAgent ($10M pre-seed, Sep 2026), Kodesage ($6.6M seed), Tessera Labs ($60M Series A, SAP upgrades).
ideas.why_they_lose: Vendors lose revenue by doing it. Retirement software sells licences, not outcomes. AI-native maintenance startups sell a cheaper replacement for the same volume, not a smaller volume with shared savings. Consultancies bill time for analysis and leave before the savings.
ideas.moat: Counter-positioning (the incumbent cannot copy it without cannibalizing); a cross-client root-cause and retirement library; a 36-month contract tail; an Internal-Audit-approved savings method (process power).
ideas.earned_secret: In a typical account a short list of applications and defects generate most tickets and stay unfixed because the billing unit is the ticket. No published repeat-ticket share was found, so the first deliverable is measuring it (delivery-practice knowledge, unverified).
ideas.first_90_days: Three design partners on unit-priced or soon-to-renew contracts; instrument their ITSM for a repeat-ticket heatmap; retire the first five zombie applications; agree the savings method with each client's Internal Audit; line up a working-capital facility to fund engineering ahead of savings.

ideas.title: Evergreen Release Utility: flat-price release remediation, Guidewire first
ideas.one_liner: A flat price per release per instance that keeps an evergreen platform estate current: predict what each vendor release breaks, patch the customer's extensions and integrations, regression-test and deploy, starting with Guidewire in P&C insurance.
ideas.customer: Guidewire reports more than 570 insurers in 43 countries; then enterprise tenants of Salesforce, ServiceNow, Workday, Oracle Fusion and Dynamics.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Insurer CIO or head of core systems signs; COO co-signs. Budget: the recurring upgrade, regression and application-management program now paid to integrators.
ideas.problem: Evergreen platforms force releases on a fixed calendar (Guidewire documents say three updates a year; other sources say two upgrades with at least one mandatory; sources conflict). Each carrier pays an integrator separately for near-identical regression and remediation; Deloitte runs a dedicated migration factory. Guidewire's Aug 2026 Qusar release sells AI agents for claims and underwriting, not release remediation. Platform vendors cannot sell upgrade services against their integrator channel, integrators bill time and materials, test-tool vendors sell seats.
ideas.solution: For each release, diff release notes against the tenant's configuration and extension inventory, predict breakage, generate patches, run an AI-maintained regression suite and deploy through the customer's pipeline, for a flat fee per release per instance with a defect-escape guarantee. Learn fix patterns across tenants that permit it (no customer data crosses tenants).
ideas.why_now: AI code and test generation is good enough for extension code; onsite certified-consultant labor got scarcer and dearer while the visa fee was in force (the fee is now vacated; whether the scarcity persists is unverified).
ideas.wedge: Ten mid-size P&C carriers (premium $1-10B) on Guidewire Cloud that are not tied to a single large integrator.
ideas.path_to_100m: Guidewire: 60 carriers (10.5% of 570) at about $1M/yr = $60M (release-driven regression and remediation spend assumed $1.5-3M/yr per carrier before a 35-50% discount; my estimate). Other platforms: 200 enterprise tenants at about $200k = $40M. Total $100M; needs roughly 10% of Guidewire's base, high for a first vertical.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Integrators (Deloitte, Cognizant, Accenture, Capgemini, Endava, TCS, Infosys, Wipro); release/test tools (Tricentis, Panaya, Opkey, Provar, Copado); Tessera Labs (SAP first, says it also covers Salesforce, Workday, Oracle); FurtherAI (Guidewire technology partner with insurance AI agents); Guidewire's own agent framework; AppFactor.
ideas.why_they_lose: The structural blockers above. But this is the most contested of the eight: Guidewire can ship the same agents, Tessera has $60M, and the cross-tenant learning claim is arguable because customers will not share configuration.
ideas.moat: Weak and honest: repeated-release data and a flat-price offer; strongest only if the platform vendor certifies the utility as a partner (a Guidewire or ServiceNow co-sell relationship would be the real moat).
ideas.earned_secret: Hypothesis to test: most breakage per release sits in a small set of extension points (integrations, custom fields, forms, rating and reporting code) that vendor release notes already list; the customer-specific part is a long tail.
ideas.first_90_days: Get Guidewire partner status; instrument one carrier's last two releases retrospectively and show predicted breakage matches actual defects; price the first flat-fee release.

ideas.title: The Foundry: wholesale AI-native delivery for the incumbents
ideas.one_liner: Sell accountable, per-unit, AI-native delivery to the IT-services firms themselves, so they can meet 25-30% price cuts with variable cost instead of a pyramid they cannot restructure.
ideas.customer: Mid-tier IT-services firms (Persistent, Coforge, Mphasis, Hexaware, LTIMindtree, Zensar, Birlasoft, Cyient, Sonata and US mid-tier peers; roughly $10B+ combined revenue for the first five, background knowledge) and delivery units of the majors.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Chief Delivery Officer or COO with the CFO. Budget: cost of revenue, replacing subcontractor spend (4% of revenue at TCS, 8.1% Infosys, 11.3% Wipro, 12.6% HCLTech in the June 2024 quarter) and bench cost.
ideas.problem: Persistent's CEO reports clients want the same work for 25-30% less; top-5 Indian firms' headcount fell 7,389 in FY26. Delivery heads' P&Ls are tied to headcount and utilization and the fresher-to-lead pyramid is a social contract. Tools exist (Devin, Copilot, internal platforms) but a tool does not change the price card or the acceptance risk, and mid-tier firms often lack integration and verification capacity.
ideas.solution: A supplier that takes whole units of work (L2/L3 tickets, regression suites, migrations, change requests) at a posted unit price with written acceptance criteria. AI-native pods plus human verifiers (displaced mid/senior engineers with pod-profit participation) return accepted outputs. The vendor keeps the client relationship and margin spread; the Foundry carries the acceptance warranty. White-label, with client flow-down for AI use and subcontracting.
ideas.why_now: Repricing wave; the new buyer is the incumbent itself (Infosys announced a Devin collaboration with Cognition on 2026-01-07 including hybrid pods and managed service inside client environments); the mid and senior layers are shrinking and available (TCS cut about 12,000 mostly mid/senior roles; senior attrition 16%); a unit that can be audited (the Meter) is now possible.
ideas.wedge: One mid-tier vendor; one unit type (L2/L3 tickets on Java, .NET, Salesforce); five of its client queues in shadow mode for 90 days, priced 35-45% below that vendor's fully loaded internal cost.
ideas.path_to_100m: A vendor with $1.5B revenue routing 5-7% of delivery ($75-105M) through the Foundry, or five vendors at 1.5-2%. One signed mid-tier anchor reaches the target, which is the speed argument; the cost is customer concentration.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Cognition (Devin) sells agents to Infosys (no evidence found of Cognizant, Wipro or HCLTech deals); Factory and others (not verified); the majors' internal platforms (TCS WisdomNext, Infosys Topaz, HCL AI Force); tier-2/3 subcontractors priced by headcount; Turing/Andela-type staffing networks; AI-native integrators selling direct (Tessera Labs).
ideas.why_they_lose: Tool vendors sell seats and leave the price card and acceptance risk with the buyer. Direct AI-native integrators compete with incumbents for the same clients so incumbents will not feed them data or queues. Internal platforms stall on headcount KPIs. Subcontractors are paid by head.
ideas.moat: Cost curve (unit price falls as the verified library grows), switching costs inside the vendor's delivery workflow, a cornered resource in senior pod partners. Honest risks: Cognition and the incumbents can move to outcomes themselves; client consent clauses can block subcontracted AI delivery; one anchor customer is one point of failure.
ideas.earned_secret: A delivery head cannot cut their own pyramid, but can sign for a subcontracted unit, because subcontracting is already 8-12% of revenue at three of the four largest firms. The supplier line is the only place in the P&L the pyramid does not defend (percentages sourced; the rest is inference).
ideas.first_90_days: Sign a letter of intent with one mid-tier vendor; define three unit types and acceptance tests; run 500 tickets in shadow; line up three senior verifiers per pod; check client consent and data-residency clauses on the five queues.

ideas.title: Hot Spare: shadow-sourcing as a service
ideas.one_liner: Pay a second, AI-native provider to shadow-run 5-10% of your live application tickets so your exit plan is tested, your price is benchmarked, and a challenger already has a foothold on the day you rebid.
ideas.customer: Regulated enterprises with critical outsourced applications: banks, insurers, asset managers, payments firms, healthcare payers. First EU-exposed US financial groups (DORA applies to EU entities including subsidiaries of US parents), then US institutions under the 2023 interagency third-party guidance (expects contingency planning; verify), then any CPO wanting price leverage.
ideas.payer_and_signer: Head of Operational Resilience or COO and the CRO sign; CIO and CPO co-sign. Budget: operational-resilience testing and vendor-risk management, plus a share of the application-management line moved to the shadow vendor.
ideas.problem: About a quarter of contracts reopen each year and clients are cutting vendor counts (Google cut $50M from HCLTech), while DORA Art. 28(8) and RTS 2024/1773 Art. 10 require documented exit strategies, tested for critical functions (secondary summaries; verify at EUR-Lex). Exit plans are paper: sample termination-for-convenience clauses run 40-85% of estimated remaining value on declining schedules plus unamortized investment, and a second vendor who is not paid to be there cannot test anything. Without a credible exit, a 25-30% price demand is a bluff.
ideas.solution: A neutral orchestrator sets up read-only copies of the client's own ticket queue, assigns 5-10% of tickets to a pre-qualified challenger in shadow (the incumbent's answer is the control), captures knowledge artifacts, and reports cost per ticket, reopen rate and time to resolve for both. After a quarter the challenger writes on low-risk tickets. Annual outputs: a DORA-style exit test report with evidence and a price-comparison pack. Revenue: orchestration/evidence fee plus margin on the shadow vendor's work.
ideas.why_now: Renegotiation wave, vendor consolidation, DORA in force since Jan 2025, and a wave of funded AI-native challengers (Tessera, AppFactor, Cognition-powered pods) that lack a way into incumbent accounts.
ideas.wedge: Three EU-exposed US banks or insurers with an operational-resilience program already testing exit; then seven more through Big 4 operational-resilience practices that need an execution partner.
ideas.path_to_100m: Per client: a 10% shadow slice of a $20M application-management contract is $2M of shadow work; at a 25% orchestrator margin plus $0.2M evidence/orchestration fees, net revenue is about $0.7M, so 143 clients; as principal on gross billings (about $2.2M per client) it is 46 clients. Addressable base roughly 750-1,000 regulated enterprises with $20M+ outsourced critical-application spend (my estimate): net view needs 14-19% share (high), gross view about 5%. Warning on paper-only exit products: NCC Group's escrow arm Escode earned only about GBP 66.5M in FY2025, grew 2%, and is being explored for sale.
ideas.who_does_it_today: Third-party-risk platforms (OneTrust, ProcessUnity, Prevalent, Archer) provide templates and registers; Big 4 operational-resilience advisory; software escrow (NCC Group/Escode, Iron Mountain); knowledge-capture tools (Kodesage, Hypercubic); in-house multi-vendor tower strategies; ISG and Everest at rebid.
ideas.why_they_lose: Incumbents cannot support their own exit; lock-in is their moat. Advisers write exit plans but do not run drills. Escrow covers code, not operating knowledge. Challengers cannot afford the unpaid pilots that a hot spare turns into paid ones.
ideas.moat: Two-sided network (challengers need a foothold, clients need a credible exit), the benchmark data it generates, and an evidence format supervisors recognize (cornered resource once two or three supervisors accept it).
ideas.earned_secret: The exit penalty, not price, is the incumbent's real moat, and exit plans are never tested because testing needs a second vendor who is not paid to be there. Paying the second vendor for a slice turns the plan from fiction into an operating fact.
ideas.first_90_days: Pick three regulated clients; stand up read-only ticket copies; pre-qualify two AI-native shadow vendors; run 5% shadow for a quarter; produce the first exit-test report and walk the client's supervisor-facing team through it. Legal checks: DORA wording at EUR-Lex and whether supervisors accept shadow-run as testing; MSAs restricting third-party access to vendor-written ticket notes (run on client-owned data); privacy and security of replicated tickets.
